scenes.title: The Counterpart of Dialectic
scenes.summary: Rhetoric is the counterpart of dialectic: both deal with what is in a way everyone's business. People examine, defend and accuse at random or by habit, so it can also be done by method, and that is the work of an art.

scenes.title: The Handbooks and the Emotions
scenes.summary: The compilers of handbooks say nothing of enthymemes, the body of proof, and teach slander, pity and anger, which are aimed at the juror, not the subject. Well-governed cities and the Areopagus forbid speaking outside the subject; the litigant need only show that the thing is so.

scenes.title: Laws Should Decide, Not Judges
scenes.summary: Rightly framed laws should define as much as possible: a few wise lawgivers are easier to find than many judges, laws are made at leisure, and the lawgiver judges the future and the universal, while members of the assembly and jurors judge present cases bound up with love, hate and interest.

scenes.title: Why the Handbooks Prefer the Courts
scenes.summary: The handbooks teach what the introduction and the narration should contain, which only puts the judge in a frame of mind. They neglect speaking in the assembly, which is nobler, because there the hearer judges his own affairs, while in the courts winning him over pays.

scenes.title: The Enthymeme
scenes.summary: The art concerns proofs, and the rhetorical demonstration is the enthymeme, a kind of syllogism; so whoever knows how syllogisms come about will be best at enthymemes. Seeing the true and what resembles it belong to the same capacity, and people are by nature fitted for the truth.

scenes.title: The Uses of Rhetoric
scenes.summary: Rhetoric is useful because the true and the just are naturally stronger, because some audiences cannot be taught, because one must be able to argue both sides to refute the unjust, and because it is shameful to be unable to defend oneself in speech. That it can be misused is true of every good except virtue.

scenes.title: Its Function
scenes.summary: Like dialectic, rhetoric has no defined subject. Its function is not to persuade but to see the available means of persuasion in each case, as medicine does what can be done for a patient; and it sees the apparent as well as the real, the sophist differing from the orator only by choice.
